title: SWE-Protégé: Small Language Models for Software Engineering Through Learned Expert Collaboration
claim: A two-phase post-training recipe teaches a small model to seek expert help and follow through, replacing aimless looping with collaborative problem solving.
layout: 2 panels: pipeline diagram left, three trajectory columns right (before, after phase 1, after phase 2)
description: The left panel (a) is a pipeline diagram. A yellow box labeled Agent System (e.g., SWE-agent) adds a new ask_expert tool to a strong LM agent. This feeds, through a blue plus node marked SFT (phase 1), into a box holding the SWE-Protégé model. A Task Dataset cylinder sits above. A lower box lists the trajectory-to-stall-and-collab reward and the patch-to-tests-and-similarity reward. These loop back through a second plus node marked GRPO (phase 2) and an Update Weights arrow. The right panel (b), separated by a dashed line, shows three color-coded trajectory snippets. The Before column is red and shows step-by-step browsing of unrelated directories. The After 1 column is light green with inconsistent expert follow-through. The After 2 column is dark green and shows a healthy ask_expert exchange. Yellow and red highlighted ask_expert callouts draw the eye.
caption: (a) Our two-phase pipeline yields SWE-Protégé-7B: Phase 1 uses SFT on expert-augmented trajectories; Phase 2 applies GRPO with trajectory-level rewards. (b) Paraphrased trajectories. Before: the SOTA SLM baseline (SWE-agent-LM-7B) fails to make reliable forward progress and degenerates into unproductive exploration. After Phase 1 : our SLM can invoke the expert, but follow-through on guidance is inconsistent and it often relapses into stalling. After Phase 2 : it learns to escalate when stalled, follow through on guidance, and report back, exhibiting multi-turn pair-programming behavior.
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) offer compelling advantages in cost, latency, and adaptability, but have lagged behind larger models on long-horizon software engineering tasks such as SWE-bench, where they suffer from pervasive action looping and low resolution rates. We introduce SWE-Protégé, a post-training framework that reframes software repair as an expert–protégé collaboration problem. In SWE-Protégé, an SLM remains the primary decision-maker while learning to selectively seek guidance from a strong expert model, recognize stalled states, and follow through on expert feedback. Our approach combines supervised fine-tuning on expert-augmented trajectories with agentic reinforcement learning that explicitly discourages degenerative looping and unproductive expert collaboration. We lightly post-train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct to achieve 42.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified with SWE-agent and Claude Opus 4.1 as the expert, a +25.4% improvement over the prior SLM state of the art, while using expert assistance sparsely (≈4 calls per task and 11% of total tokens). With Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the expert, it reaches 41.0% at a median expert API cost of USD 0.15 per task, 8.2× lower than running the expert alone.
